description: One starter book per interest with 20 reading cards per book.

cards.title: If You Have to Explain It, It's Broken
cards.idea: You watch someone reach for your product, then stop and look around for help.
cards.description: They didn't open your app to learn. They opened it to do something. The pause happens before they even try. Now they're scanning for clues, and every second makes them trust it less. People skip instructions when they're already moving. Hesitation is confusion wearing a polite face. The moment you need to explain is the moment you already lost.

cards.title: Clarity Beats Cleverness
cards.idea: You designed a hidden gesture that feels like magic. Users swipe right past it every time.
cards.description: The shortcut that seemed playful in the prototype now just confuses people who want to move forward. They're not exploring. They're trying to finish. That clever moment you loved becomes the place where they give up. Dull choices feel safe when you're rushed. Clever choices feel risky when you're uncertain. You designed it to impress yourself, not to get out of the way.

cards.title: The Object Should Tell You What to Do
cards.idea: They push the door. It says pull. They try again, harder.
cards.description: The handle looks like something you grab and pull, so they pull. But the door was designed to push. Now they're standing there feeling stupid, and the door just collected another victim. Shape tells people what to do before they think. When form lies, people trust themselves less. A silent object forces guessing. Guessing feels like failure.

cards.title: Errors Are Designed In
cards.idea: Seventeen people this week hit delete instead of save. You blame them for not being careful.
cards.description: The buttons sit next to each other, same size, same color. The system baited them into clicking wrong, then punished them for doing exactly what the layout suggested. That's not user error. That's design shipping consequences. When the same mistake repeats, it's a feature you didn't plan for. Ambiguous layouts are silent invitations to fail. Blaming users for predictable behavior is just expensive denial.

cards.title: Feedback Is How Systems Speak
cards.idea: You tap submit. Nothing happens. You tap again. Now you've submitted twice.
cards.description: The system was processing the first tap, but it never told you. So you guessed, acted, and broke something. Silence doesn't feel like patience. It feels like failure. No signal makes people repeat the action. Bad news is still better than nothing. When the system goes quiet, users write their own story. It's never good.

cards.title: People Don't Read Your Manual
cards.idea: They click three things, decide how it works, and never update that mental model again.
cards.description: You built it one way. They guessed another. Now they're using your product wrong, and they'll keep using it wrong because their model is already set. The gap between what you meant and what they learned is permanent. Users build their theory while moving, not while reading. The wrong model sticks harder than the right one. When their model breaks, they don't blame the model. They blame themselves.

cards.title: Signifiers Are the Real Instructions
cards.idea: The door opens both ways. The handle only exists on one side. Everyone pulls.
cards.description: It can push and pull, but the handle screams pull. That's a signifier lying to you. People don't read affordances. They read signals. Remove the signal, and they stand there stuck. Add the wrong signal, and they try the wrong thing with full confidence. Affordances are what's possible. Signifiers are what gets tried. Missing signals create hesitation. Wrong signals create certainty in failure. You're not designing what it can do. You're designing what it looks like it does.

cards.title: Constraints Make Things Easier
cards.idea: You flip the USB plug three times before it finally fits. Now it only goes in one way.
cards.description: The old plug gave you two chances to be wrong. The new one removes the choice entirely. You can't fail because there's no wrong option left. Constraints aren't restrictions. They're decisions made upstream so you don't have to. Physical limits block wrong moves before they happen. Less freedom means less time spent guessing. The best constraint is the one you don't notice because the wrong thing was never possible.

cards.title: The Gulf Between Wanting and Doing
cards.idea: You know what you want to do. You just can't figure out how to make the system do it.
cards.description: There's the goal in your head and the maze of buttons in front of you. Somewhere between the two is a translation you can't figure out. You try three approaches, none of them work, and now you're convinced the product just can't do it. Small gaps feel natural. Large gaps feel like the product is fighting you. The distance between wanting and doing is measured in abandoned attempts. Good design closes the gap before you notice it existed.

cards.title: What You Can't Find Doesn't Exist
cards.idea: You spent two weeks building the export feature. No one uses it because it's buried in settings.
cards.description: They looked for it once, didn't see it, and decided your product can't do exports. The feature works perfectly. It's just invisible. Now you're getting feature requests for something you already built. People scan for five seconds, then decide what's possible. Buried features die in silence. If it takes more than two clicks to discover, it's not a feature. It's a secret.

cards.title: Slips and Mistakes Are Different Problems
cards.idea: You reach for save and hit delete. Then you confidently choose the wrong workflow entirely.
cards.description: The first one is a slip—your hand misfired. The second is a mistake—your mental model was wrong from the start. You fix slips with better buttons. You fix mistakes with better explanations. Treat them the same, and you fix nothing. Slips are execution errors. Mistakes are planning errors. A slip looks like a tremor. A mistake looks like confidence. Most products only defend against one and wonder why the other keeps happening.

cards.title: Put the Knowledge in the World
cards.idea: The pilot forgets a step mid-flight. The checklist doesn't. The plane lands safely.
cards.description: Memory is fast when it works and useless when it fails. Labels, signs, and checklists don't forget. They don't get distracted. They don't assume. That's why cockpits rely on paper, not recall. Memory is unreliable under pressure. Visible information never fails. The best systems let you remember when you can and read when you can't.

cards.title: When Everyone Fails, It's the System
cards.idea: Fifty people this month made the same error. You keep blaming the users.
cards.description: One person makes a mistake, maybe they weren't paying attention. Fifty people make the same mistake, and you're still calling it human error. That's not carelessness. That's the system teaching them to fail. One failure is an accident. Repeated failure is design. Asking "who messed up" is cheaper than asking "why did the system let them". The product that expects perfection is the one that punishes normal behavior.

cards.title: Good Design Disappears
cards.idea: You opened a hundred doors this year. You remember the one that stuck.
cards.description: The doors that worked didn't even register. You just walked through. The one that confused you, that one stays in memory. Good design earns nothing. Bad design earns a reputation. Things that work don't get noticed. Things that break get remembered. The best design feels like no design at all.

cards.title: Controls Should Mirror the Thing They Control
cards.idea: Four burners in a square. Four knobs in a row. You turn the wrong one and burn your hand.
cards.description: The burners are arranged like a grid, but the knobs are lined up like a queue. Now every time you cook, you're translating spatial logic in your head. That's not a learning curve. That's a permanent tax. Good mapping makes the connection obvious. Bad mapping forces mental translation every single time. You keep guessing because the layout keeps lying.

cards.title: Make the Dangerous Thing Hard to Do
cards.idea: The microwave door is open. You press start. Nothing happens. You're annoyed, but not burnt.
cards.description: The interlock feels like friction until you realize what it just prevented. A car that won't shift out of park without the brake. A delete button that asks twice. These aren't obstacles. They're guardrails at the exact moment you're most likely to wreck. Interlocks block action until it's safe. Annoyance now beats catastrophe later. The dangerous path should feel harder than the safe one.

cards.title: Memory Is the Wrong Storage System
cards.idea: You ask users to remember six options. They show up distracted and forget three.
cards.description: They're not focused. They're mid-conversation, mid-task, mid-life. Working memory holds maybe four things, and it's already holding what they had for lunch and where they parked. You want them to remember your sequence too. They won't. Memory is tiny and already busy. Recognition beats recall every time. If your design depends on memory, it depends on luck.

cards.title: Complexity and Confusion Are Not the Same
cards.idea: A pilot flies a plane with a thousand switches. You can't figure out your TV remote.
cards.description: The cockpit is complex because flying is hard. The remote is confusing because someone organized eight buttons poorly. Complexity lives in the task. Confusion lives in the design. One is necessary. The other is just lazy. Complex systems can still feel clear. Simple systems can feel impossible. The goal isn't to remove complexity. It's to stop creating confusion.

cards.title: Symptoms Lie, Root Causes Hide
cards.idea: Users keep hitting the wrong button. You make the label bigger. They still hit the wrong button.
cards.description: The symptom was the mistake. The root cause was why the button was confusing in the first place. You fixed the surface and left the structure broken. Now you're just patching symptoms faster than they appear. The first explanation is always the visible one. The real problem is usually three layers deeper. Patching symptoms is how technical debt compounds in silence.

cards.title: Design for the Person Who Isn't Paying Attention
cards.idea: Your user is on a phone call, holding coffee, and walking. They're not reading your tooltip.
cards.description: They're not giving you their full attention because they never had it to give. They're tired, distracted, or just passing through. You designed for someone focused and calm. That person doesn't exist. No one arrives with full attention. The real test is whether it works mid-distraction. Design for the exhausted user. The alert one will be fine.
